name: Software Development Security
plainMeaning: This domain is about building security into software from the first idea until the day it is retired. It also teaches you how to judge the safety of software you buy, borrow or rent from others.

topics.name: Software development life cycle and methods
topics.simpleExplanation: Software is built in steps. You plan it, design it, write it, test it, release it, run it and finally retire it. That journey is called the software development life cycle. Teams follow different methods, such as waterfall, agile or DevOps. Some move slowly through fixed stages. Others deliver small pieces very often. The method can change, but one rule stays the same. Security must start at the very beginning and continue at every step. Adding it at the end costs more and works less well.

studyNotes.heading: The life cycle, stage by stage
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to walk through the whole life of a piece of software, from the first idea to the day it is retired.

The software development life cycle, or SDLC, is that full journey. Books name the stages in slightly different ways, so learn the order of the ideas and not one exact set of labels. Here is the order.

- Plan and gather requirements.
- Design.
- Develop.
- Test.
- Deploy.
- Operate and maintain.
- Retire.

Think of building a house. First you decide what the family needs. Then an architect draws the plans. Builders put it up. An inspector checks it. The family moves in. For years the family repairs it and looks after it. One day it is pulled down, and the site is cleared.

Now let us follow a workplace example, a school fees portal where parents pay online. In planning, the team writes down what the portal must do. It also classifies the data, which means deciding how sensitive it is. Card details and children's records are highly sensitive. In design, the team decides how the parts fit together. In development, programmers write the code. In testing, the team proves that the features work and that the security controls work. In deployment, the portal is released through an approved process. In operation, staff patch it, which means applying fixes, and they watch it and control changes to it. In retirement, the portal is switched off, and its data is kept or destroyed according to policy.

Two words belong at the deployment stage. Certification is the technical check that the controls meet the requirements. Accreditation is management's formal acceptance of the system and its remaining risk. Someone technical certifies. A senior manager accredits.

Notice that retirement is a real stage. Old software that nobody owns keeps running, goes unpatched and still holds data. A forgotten system is an open door.

Here is what to take away. Software has a whole life, from planning to retirement, and someone must own its security at every stage.

studyNotes.heading: Security at each stage, and shifting left
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at the security job that belongs to each stage, and at why doing that job early saves so much money.

In planning, you write security requirements next to the business requirements. For example, the system must lock an account after repeated failed logins. In design, you do threat modeling, which means listing what could go wrong before anything is built. You also write abuse cases, which describe how someone might misuse a feature. In development, programmers follow secure coding rules, and a second person reviews the code. In testing, you check the security controls on purpose. Do not copy real customer data into a test system without protecting it. Masking, which hides the real values, or made-up data is safer. In deployment, you harden the system, which means removing what is not needed and setting safe options. In operation, you patch, monitor and control change. In retirement, you remove accounts and dispose of the data safely.

Now for the money. Think of moving a wall in a house. On paper, it costs an eraser. After the family moves in, it costs a builder, a plumber and a painter.

Here is a worked example. The figures are made up, simply to show the idea. Suppose a flaw would cost 100 dollars to fix during design. If it is found in testing, the code must be changed and tested again, so suppose it costs 1,500 dollars. If it is found after release, there is an emergency patch, customer notices and perhaps a breach, so suppose it costs 10,000 dollars. Ten thousand divided by one hundred is one hundred. The same flaw has cost one hundred times as much, only because it was found late.

Moving security work to earlier stages is called shifting left. Picture the stages written from left to right on a whiteboard. Planning is on the left.

A workplace team might add one hour of threat modeling to each new feature. That hour is cheap, and it removes whole families of problems.

Here is your takeaway. Every stage has a security task, and the earlier a flaw is found, the less it costs to fix.

studyNotes.heading: Waterfall and spiral
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at two older methods that are still tested, waterfall and spiral.

A development method is simply the way a team organizes its work through the life cycle.

Waterfall runs the stages in strict order. Each stage is finished and signed off before the next one begins. Think of water going over a series of ledges. It does not flow back up. A later version allows a step back to the stage just before, but the idea is the same.

Waterfall suits projects where the requirements are stable and well known. It also suits work that needs heavy paperwork and formal approval. A workplace example is a small tax calculation system, where the rules are fixed by law.

Its weakness is that users see the product late, so problems also appear late. Security fits through written requirements at the start and a formal review at the end of each stage.

The spiral model repeats a loop many times. Picture a spiral on a page, growing wider with each turn. Each loop has four activities, in this order.

- Set the goals for this loop.
- Study the risks and deal with them.
- Build and test a prototype, which is an early trial version.
- Plan the next loop.

Think of a family designing a new kitchen. They first make a cardboard model, and they notice that the door hits the cupboard. They fix that problem before spending real money. Then they try a fuller model, and so on.

A workplace example is a first-of-its-kind medical device. Nobody knows yet whether the design will work. Each loop answers the biggest open risk, and leaders can stop before spending more.

Spiral suits large, uncertain and risky projects. Its weakness is cost and complexity, because the risk analysis needs skilled people.

On the exam, watch for the clue words. Stable requirements and strict stages suggest waterfall. Risk-driven work and prototypes suggest spiral.

Here is what to take away. Waterfall is strict order for stable needs. Spiral is repeated loops of risk analysis and prototypes for uncertain needs.

studyNotes.heading: Agile and Scrum
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at agile, which is the way most software teams work today, and at Scrum, its best-known form.

Agile is a family of methods that deliver small working pieces in short cycles and welcome change. It is built on the Agile Manifesto, which states four values. Learn all four.

- Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
- Working software over comprehensive documentation.
- Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
- Responding to change over following a plan.

The things on the right still have value. The things on the left simply have more.

Think of cooking for friends. You could plan the whole menu a month ahead and serve it no matter what. Or you could cook one dish, let them taste it, and adjust the next one. Agile is the tasting approach.

Scrum is a popular agile method. Work happens in sprints, which are fixed cycles of one month or less. The backlog is the ordered list of work still to be done. The product owner decides the order of that list. The Scrum master helps the team follow the method and removes obstacles. The developers build the product. Each sprint ends with a review of what was built, and a retrospective, where the team talks about how to work better.

Now for security. Agile does not forbid security, but speed can push it aside. Here is how a workplace team keeps it in. Picture a bank's mobile app team. It places security needs in the backlog as real work items. For a new money transfer feature, it adds an abuse case, such as someone sending a thousand small transfers to hide a theft. Its definition of done, which is the agreed list of what finished means, includes passing the security checks. A security champion, a developer with extra security training, sits inside the team.

Do not read working software over documentation as no documentation. Audits and accountability still need records.

Here is your takeaway. Agile means small pieces and fast feedback, and security must be built into the backlog and the definition of done.

studyNotes.heading: Scaled agile, DevOps and DevSecOps
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at how agile grows to fit large organizations, and at how development, operations and security come together.

One Scrum team is small. A large product may need dozens of teams. The Scaled Agile Framework, or SAFe, coordinates many agile teams working on one product. Teams are grouped into an Agile Release Train, a long-lived team of teams, usually 50 to 125 people. They plan together in a planning interval, usually 8 to 12 weeks.

Think of many cooks preparing one wedding banquet. Each cook has a dish, but the dishes must arrive together and match. Security fits SAFe through shared standards and architecture, so that each team does not invent its own rules.

DevOps joins development and operations into one way of working. In the past, programmers threw finished code over a wall, and the operations staff had to run it. DevOps removes that wall. It relies on automation to build, test and release often. A workplace example is an online shop that releases small changes several times a day. If a change fails, it is quickly rolled back, meaning undone.

DevSecOps adds security as the shared duty of everyone. Security checks run automatically on each change. Security staff write rules and tools, and help the teams use them. Security is no longer one gate at the end.

Let us walk through one change in a DevSecOps team, step by step. A developer saves a change. A tool immediately reads the code for known flaws. Another tool checks the outside components for known problems. The build fails if a serious problem appears, and the developer fixes it within minutes. The change then goes to a test system, where it is attacked by an automated scanner. Only then may it reach production.

Be clear about one thing. Buying tools does not create DevSecOps. It is a change of culture, so it needs management support and shared responsibility.

Here is what to take away. SAFe coordinates many agile teams, DevOps joins building and running, and DevSecOps makes security everyone's automated, everyday work.

studyNotes.heading: Choosing a method and thinking like an adviser
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will bring the methods together and practice the way of thinking that the exam rewards.

First, no method is secure on its own. Waterfall can produce insecure software, and so can DevSecOps. What matters is whether security requirements, reviews, testing and sign-off exist inside the method that the team really uses.

Second, the method is a business decision. You are an adviser. Think of a mechanic asked about a family's choice of car. A good mechanic does not insist that everyone drive the same model. A good mechanic asks how the car will be used, and then makes sure that it is safe.

So, when a question offers an answer that says to force the team back to a different method, be careful. That answer is usually wrong, unless the scenario shows that the method truly cannot fit. Work with the method the business has chosen, and build security into it.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital runs two projects. One replaces a fixed billing formula required by regulation. The other builds a new patient app whose features will change as patients respond. The adviser accepts a waterfall approach for the first, with reviews at each stage. The adviser accepts an agile approach for the second, with security items in the backlog. Different methods, same security outcomes.

Now here is a simple order of thought for scenario questions.

- Ask where in the life cycle the scenario sits.
- Ask what security activity belongs at that point.
- Look for the answer that fixes the cause in the process, not just the single symptom.
- Make sure that management makes the risk decisions.

People come first as well. If software controls a train or a medical pump, safety outweighs the delivery date.

Finally, keep the words straight. Certification is technical. Accreditation is a management decision. Sprints belong to Scrum. Prototypes and risk loops belong to spiral.

Here is your takeaway. Do not argue for one best method. Help the business choose what fits, and make sure that security is built in, whichever method it chooses.

question.prompt: A bank's development team has moved to two-week sprints. The security team's manual review, held just before each release, can no longer keep up. Releases are now being delayed. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Skip the security review for low-value releases until staffing improves
Put security needs in the backlog and automate tests in each build
Return the team to waterfall so that the review stage has enough time
Hold the security review once a year and accept the risk between reviews
question.explanation: Building security needs and automated tests into the normal work fixes the cause, so security keeps pace with delivery. Going back to waterfall is tempting, but it changes the business's chosen method and does not make security part of the work. Skipping reviews simply removes the control.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A government agency is starting a new benefits payment system. The project manager asks when the system's security needs should first be written down. What is the BEST answer?
options: After the code is written, so that testers know what to check
During requirements, alongside the business needs
Just before deployment, as part of the accreditation package
During the first maintenance cycle, once real threats are seen
practiceQuestions.explanation: Security needs belong with the other requirements at the very start, so that they shape the design and cost less. Writing them before accreditation is tempting because that is when management signs, but by then it is far too late to build them in.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Technical staff have confirmed that the controls on a new claims system meet the requirements. Some risk remains. What must happen BEFORE the system goes live?
options: The developers sign a statement that the remaining risk is small
The testers repeat the checks until no risk remains at all
The security team accepts the remaining risk for the business
A senior manager formally accepts the remaining risk
practiceQuestions.explanation: That formal acceptance is accreditation, and it is a management decision. Having the security team accept the risk is tempting, but security staff advise and do not own business risk. No amount of testing brings risk to zero.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A utility needs a small billing calculator. The rules are fixed by regulation and will not change. The regulator also expects formal sign-off documents at the end of each stage. Which development method is the BEST fit?
options: Waterfall
Scrum
Spiral
DevOps
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stable requirements and formal sign-off at each stage are what waterfall is built for. Spiral is tempting because the work is regulated, but spiral is meant for uncertain projects with major risks to explore.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A product owner writes a work item that lets customers reset their passwords by email. Before the team builds it, the security adviser wants the team to think about how the feature could be misused. Which technique BEST does this?
options: A regression test run after the feature has been released
A service level agreement agreed with the email provider
An abuse case added alongside the work item
A change request raised during the maintenance stage
practiceQuestions.explanation: An abuse case describes how someone might misuse a feature, so it shapes the work before it is built. A regression test is tempting because it is a security activity, but it happens after the work and only checks what was already built.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A car maker has twelve agile teams building one vehicle software platform. Each team has invented its own security rules, and the parts often fail when they are joined together. What should the security manager recommend?
options: Ask each team to write a stronger security policy of its own
Move every team back onto a single waterfall project plan
Coordinate the teams under a scaled framework and shared standards
Let each team keep its rules and test only the final product
practiceQuestions.explanation: A scaled agile approach with shared standards and architecture fixes the cause, which is a lack of coordination. Going back to waterfall is tempting, but it changes the business's chosen method and does not by itself create common security rules.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company announces that it has adopted DevSecOps and buys scanning tools. Developers ignore the results, saying that security belongs to the security team. What is the MOST important next step?
options: Gain management backing for shared ownership of security
Buy a second scanner to confirm the results of the first
Remove the scanners and return to a final review by security staff
Have the security staff fix all of the reported flaws themselves
practiceQuestions.explanation: DevSecOps is a change of culture, so leaders must make security a shared duty. Having security staff fix the flaws is tempting because the work gets done, but it keeps the same divide that caused the problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software firm finds most of its serious flaws during final testing, and the rework regularly delays its releases. Which change would BEST reduce this problem?
options: Add more testers to the final testing stage of each project
Delay every release by one month to allow more rework
Hire outside penetration testers to check every release
Add threat modeling during design
practiceQuestions.explanation: Threat modeling during design finds problems before they are built, which is shifting left. More testers are tempting, but they still find the flaws at the late, expensive stage.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During testing of a new insurance system, a project team wants to copy live customer records into the test environment to make the tests realistic. What should the security adviser recommend?
options: Allow it, as long as all testers sign a confidentiality agreement
Use masked or made-up data instead of the real records
Allow it, because the test network sits inside the firewall
Copy the records, and delete them when the project closes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Masked or made-up data allows realistic testing without exposing real people's records. A confidentiality agreement is tempting, but test systems usually have weaker controls and wider access, so the data would still be at risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A retailer is replacing an old order system that holds many years of customer data. What should the security manager ensure as the system is retired?
options: Retention rules are applied, and the rest is securely destroyed
The server is switched off and stored with its disks intact
The old servers are given to staff after a quick disk format
The system keeps running in case someone needs an old record
practiceQuestions.explanation: Retirement means keeping only what policy and law require, and safely destroying the rest. Storing the server is tempting because nothing is lost, but the data stays exposed and no one is managing it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A project lead insists that every design must be fully documented before anyone writes any working code. Which Agile Manifesto value does this attitude MOST directly conflict with?
options: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Responding to change over following a plan
practiceQuestions.explanation: Putting documents ahead of working code runs against the value of working software over comprehensive documentation. Responding to change is tempting, because the attitude is also rigid, but the conflict stated here is about documentation.

topics.name: Maturity models and running software
topics.simpleExplanation: A maturity model is a ladder. It shows how well an organization builds software and what the next step up looks like. After software goes live, the longest part of its life begins. It must be patched, watched and carefully changed. A change process stops people from making risky changes without permission. An integrated product team brings developers, security staff, operations and business people together from the start. Together, these ideas turn good software work from luck into a habit.

studyNotes.heading: What a maturity model is, and the five CMMI levels
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to learn what a maturity model is, and then the five levels you need to know in exact order.

A maturity model measures how repeatable and how well managed an organization's work is. It is a ladder. It tells you where you stand, and what the next step looks like.

Think of learning to cook. At first, a meal turns out well only by luck. Later you follow a recipe for each meal. Then the family writes one recipe book that everyone uses. Then you weigh everything and time everything. Finally, you keep adjusting the recipes based on those measurements.

The Capability Maturity Model Integration, or CMMI, grew from the older Capability Maturity Model, or CMM, which was first written for software. Here are the five levels, from lowest to highest.

- Level 1, Initial: work is chaotic and reactive. Success depends on a few heroes.
- Level 2, Managed: each project is planned and tracked.
- Level 3, Defined: one standard process is used across the whole organization.
- Level 4, Quantitatively Managed: the process is measured and controlled with numbers.
- Level 5, Optimizing: the organization keeps improving, using what it measures.

There is a memory aid in your notes for this order. I Must Decide Quickly, Often. Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.

Some newer versions of the model also describe a level zero, called Incomplete. The five levels above are the ladder to learn.

A maturity level describes how good the process is. It does not prove that a particular product is secure. A Level 5 company can still ship a flaw. But it is more likely to catch it, learn from it and stop it happening again.

Also, you cannot sensibly skip rungs. You cannot measure a standard process with numbers until you actually have a standard process.

Here is what to take away. Maturity is about repeatable process, and the order is Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.

studyNotes.heading: Climbing the ladder, and the old names
studyNotes.body:
Now we will climb the ladder with one worked example, and clear up a naming trap that catches many people.

Picture a small company that builds software for pharmacies.

At first, one brilliant developer holds everything in her head. When she is on holiday, releases fail. That is Level 1, Initial.

The company's managers begin to plan each project, track its progress and record its requirements. One project may run differently from another, but each is under control. That is Level 2, Managed.

Next, the company writes one standard process, including secure coding rules and code review. Every team follows it, and new projects start from it. That is Level 3, Defined.

Then leaders begin to measure. They track how many defects are found per thousand lines of code, and how long flaws stay open. They use these numbers to control the process and to predict results. That is Level 4, Quantitatively Managed.

Finally, the company studies those numbers and tries improvements. It finds that most flaws come from one type of input handling, so it changes its training and tools. That is Level 5, Optimizing.

Now for the trap. The older CMM used these names: Initial, Repeatable, Defined, Managed, Optimizing. So the word Managed is Level 4 in the old model, and Level 2 in CMMI. Repeatable, in the old model, is Level 2. If a question says Repeatable, it is using the older names.

There is also a simple model for carrying out improvement, known as IDEAL. Its five phases come in this order.

- Initiating: build the reason and the support for change.
- Diagnosing: find out where you stand.
- Establishing: set priorities and a plan.
- Acting: carry out the plan.
- Learning: review what happened and prepare for the next round.

As a manager, remember that the move from one level to the next is a business investment. Not every organization needs Level 5.

Here is your takeaway. Project-by-project is Managed, one standard for all is Defined, and numbers mean Quantitatively Managed. Watch the word Managed in the older model.

studyNotes.heading: SAMM: maturity for software security
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at a maturity model made specifically for software security.

CMMI looks at process quality in general. The Software Assurance Maturity Model, or SAMM, looks directly at software security. It comes from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a community that publishes free security guidance. SAMM is free and open for anyone to use.

SAMM has five business functions. Learn these five.

- Governance.
- Design.
- Implementation.
- Verification.
- Operations.

Each function holds three security practices, so there are fifteen practices in all. Governance covers strategy and metrics, policy and compliance, and education and guidance. Design covers threat assessment, security requirements and security architecture. Implementation covers secure build, secure deployment and defect management. Verification covers architecture assessment, requirements-driven testing and security testing. Operations covers incident management, environment management and operational management.

Each practice is scored at a maturity level from 1 to 3. A higher score means the activity is more complete and more consistent.

Think of a health check at the doctor. You do not get one single mark for your body. You get readings for heart, blood and eyesight. Then you agree which to improve first.

Here is a worked example of the steps. An insurance company assesses itself. It scores 2 for security requirements, but only 1 for security testing. Its applications handle sensitive medical data, so it sets a target of 2 for security testing within one year. It builds a plan, carries it out and measures again. Notice that the company does not chase a 3 everywhere. A small charity with a simple website could rightly set much lower targets. The target should match the risk.

You may also meet BSIMM, the Building Security In Maturity Model. BSIMM is descriptive. It reports what real companies are doing. SAMM is prescriptive. It suggests what you should do and how to improve.

Here is what to take away. SAMM measures software security across five functions and fifteen practices, on a scale of 1 to 3, with targets set by risk.

studyNotes.heading: Operations and maintenance
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at the longest stage in the life of software, the years after it goes live.

Most of the life of software happens after release. This is called operation and maintenance. A common mistake is to treat release day as the end of the security work. It is closer to the beginning.

Think of owning a car. Buying it is a single day. After that come years of oil changes, tire checks, repairs and new rules from the licensing office. If you stop all that, the car does not stay as safe as the day you bought it.

Software is the same, even though the code does not wear out. Threats change. A flaw nobody knew about last year may be widely known today. So software that was safe last year may not be safe now.

The work includes applying patches, which are fixes from the developer or the vendor. It includes monitoring logs and alerts, and scanning for new weaknesses. It includes reviewing who still has access. It includes keeping backups, responding to incidents, and planning for the end of support and for retirement.

Here is a workplace example. A city council runs a parking payment system. A serious flaw is announced in a component that it uses. Because it has good operations, it knows where that component runs. It tests the patch, gets emergency approval and applies it within a day. It then checks the logs for signs that someone used the flaw before it was patched.

End of support deserves special attention. When a vendor stops issuing patches for a product, every new flaw stays open forever. The right response is to plan an upgrade or a replacement, and to manage the risk until then, perhaps with network isolation and closer monitoring. Working fine today is not a reason to ignore it.

Hot fixes must go back into the main code as well. If they do not, the next release quietly brings the old flaw back.

Here is your takeaway. Security continues after release, through patching, monitoring, access review and planning for the end of support.

studyNotes.heading: Change management
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how changes to software are controlled, because uncontrolled change is one of the most common causes of outages and security failures.

Change management makes sure that each change is requested, approved, tested and recorded. Learn its three parts in this order.

- Request control: users ask for changes. Managers weigh cost and benefit and set priorities.
- Change control: developers build and test the change in an orderly way, with a way to undo it.
- Release control: the finished change is approved for production. Acceptance testing happens here, and debugging code must be removed.

Think of having a kitchen wall removed. First you ask, and you decide whether it is worth the cost. Then the builder does the job carefully, with a plan for what to do if a pipe is found. Finally, an inspector approves the work before the family uses the room.

Here is a workplace walk-through. A payroll clerk asks for a new report. That is the request. A manager compares cost and benefit and gives it a priority. A group called the change advisory board reviews the risk. A developer builds the report on a test system, and another person reviews the code. Testers confirm that it works and that nothing else broke. The release team, not the developer, moves it to production. Records are updated, and the change can be undone if necessary.

Developers should not move their own code into production. This is separation of duties, which means splitting a task so that no single person can complete it alone. Even small teams can have a second authorized person approve and deploy.

Emergency changes are still controlled. An authorized person approves, the change is tested as far as time allows, and full records and review follow soon after. Speed changes the timing of the paperwork. It does not remove the control.

Do not confuse this with configuration management, which records the exact versions and settings in use. Change management controls how they change.

Here is what to take away. Request, then change, then release. Separate the duties, and keep control even in an emergency.

studyNotes.heading: Integrated product teams
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at a way of organizing people, called an integrated product team, and bring this topic together.

An integrated product team, or IPT, brings people from many fields into one team for the whole project. Members may include developers, security, operations, quality, legal, purchasing and the business owner. They share responsibility for the result.

Think of planning a family wedding. If the cook, the florist, the driver and the person paying all meet from the start, you learn early that the road is closed and the hall has no oven. If each works alone, you find out on the day.

Here is a workplace example. A government department is building a new licensing system. The old way passes the work along a line. Business people write requirements. Developers build. Then, near the end, security reviews it, and the legal team finds that the data cannot be stored overseas. Months of work are wasted.

With an integrated product team, the lawyer raises the data location rule in the first week. The security specialist helps to shape the design. The purchasing officer checks that the supplier contract includes security duties. The operations lead makes sure that the system can be monitored and patched. Problems surface early, because each point of view is in the room.

How does this compare with DevOps? DevOps joins mainly development and operations, and leans heavily on automation. An integrated product team is usually wider, and includes business, legal and purchasing roles. It is mostly about how people are organized around a product.

The team needs a clear leader and clear decision rights, because shared responsibility can turn into nobody's responsibility. Risk acceptance still sits with the accountable manager.

Now let us tie the whole topic together. Maturity models tell you how good your process is. Operations and maintenance keep the software safe through its long working life. Change management stops risky surprises. And integrated teams bring the right people together early.

Here is your takeaway. An integrated product team puts many fields together from the start, so that problems are found while they are cheap to fix.

keyTerms.meaning: Capability Maturity Model Integration: a five-level model of process maturity.
One standard process is used across the whole organization.
The process is measured and controlled with numbers.
Software Assurance Maturity Model: an open model from OWASP that measures software security practices.
The part of change management where changes are asked for and prioritized.
The part where changes are built and tested in an orderly way.
The part where changes are accepted and approved for production.
Splitting a task so that one person cannot complete it alone.
Integrated Product Team: people from many fields sharing one project from the start.

keyPoints: CMMI levels run Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.
SAMM has five business functions and focuses on software security.
Change management runs request control, change control, then release control.
Emergency changes are still approved, recorded and reviewed.
An integrated product team includes many fields from the start.

question.prompt: A hospital's software group has written one standard development process. Every project team now follows it. Leaders have not yet started to measure the process with numbers. Which CMMI level BEST describes the group?
options: Initial
Managed
Quantitatively Managed
Defined
question.explanation: One standard process used across the organization is the mark of Level 3, Defined. Managed is tempting, but that level only means each project is planned and tracked. Quantitatively Managed needs numeric measurement, which has not started.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An old policy document says that the company aims for Level 2, Repeatable, of the Capability Maturity Model. A manager wants to update the wording to match CMMI. What is Level 2 called in CMMI?
options: Initial
Defined
Managed
Optimizing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Level 2 in CMMI is Managed, which replaced the older name Repeatable. Defined is tempting because it sounds like the next idea, but it is Level 3 in both models.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A start-up's software releases succeed only when its lead engineer is working. Nothing is written down, and each release is handled differently. Which CMMI level BEST describes this company?
options: Initial
Managed
Defined
Optimizing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Chaotic work that depends on heroes is Level 1, Initial. Managed is tempting because someone is clearly in charge, but Level 2 requires each project to be planned and tracked.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has reached CMMI Level 3, and all of its teams use one standard process. What must the company do to reach the NEXT level?
options: Write one standard process for all of its teams to follow
Plan and track each of its projects on an individual basis
Rely on experienced staff to solve problems as they arise
Measure its process and control it with numbers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Level 4, Quantitatively Managed, means that the process is measured and controlled with numbers. Writing one standard process is tempting, but that is what the company has already done to reach Level 3.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager wants a free, open model that scores an organization's software security practices and helps it to set improvement targets. Which of these BEST fits?
options: The seven-step NIST Risk Management Framework
The OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System ratings
A software bill of materials for each product
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Software Assurance Maturity Model is free, comes from OWASP and scores software security practices. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System is tempting because it gives scores, but it rates individual flaws and does not measure an organization's practices.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A small charity completes a Software Assurance Maturity Model assessment and scores 1 in most practices. Its board asks whether it must reach a score of 3 everywhere. What is the BEST advice?
options: Yes, because any score below 3 means that the model has been failed
No, because the model applies only to very large software firms
No, because targets should match its own risk and resources
Yes, but the charity may take up to ten years to get there
practiceQuestions.explanation: The model expects each organization to set targets that match its risk. Saying that it applies only to large firms is tempting because the charity is small, but any organization may use it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An insurer's assessment looks at its threat assessment, security requirements and security architecture practices. Which Software Assurance Maturity Model business function is being assessed?
options: Governance
Design
Verification
Operations
practiceQuestions.explanation: Those three practices make up the Design function. Verification is tempting because it sounds like assessment, but its practices are architecture assessment, requirements-driven testing and security testing.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A user asks for a new report in a payroll application. A manager has weighed the cost and benefit and has given the request a priority. Which part of change management comes NEXT?
options: Change control
Release control
Request control
Configuration audit
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order is request control, change control, then release control. Request control has just finished, so developers now build and test the change. Release control is tempting, but nothing has been built yet.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A developer has finished a tested change. The release manager is on leave, so the developer asks to move the code into production personally. What is the BEST response?
options: Allow it, since the code has already passed all of its tests
Allow it, then have the developer write a short note about it
Delay every change until the release manager is back from leave
Have another authorized person approve and deploy the change
practiceQuestions.explanation: A second authorized person keeps separation of duties and lets the work continue. Delaying every change is tempting because it is safe, but it harms the business when a proper alternative exists.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A vendor has ended support for the platform under a seven-year-old application. The application still works well and has had no incidents. What should the security manager do?
options: Leave it unchanged, because no incident has happened so far
Record it in the risk register and close the matter for good
Plan an upgrade or replacement and manage the risk until then
Ask the application's users to report anything that looks odd
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without vendor patches, each new flaw stays open, so the manager must plan a way out and reduce the risk meanwhile. Recording it in the register is tempting, but recording a risk does nothing to treat it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A defense program keeps discovering, late in each project, that legal and purchasing requirements were missed and that security was never consulted. Which approach would BEST address the cause?
options: Form an integrated product team from the start
Hold a review meeting when each product is finished
Move all of the developers under the operations manager
Ask the legal team to write a longer list of requirements
practiceQuestions.explanation: An integrated product team puts legal, purchasing, security and others together from the beginning. A review meeting at the end is tempting, but it finds the same problems at the same late stage.

topics.name: Security controls in development ecosystems
topics.simpleExplanation: Software is made in a kind of workshop. The workshop holds languages, ready-made code, tools, automatic build lines and storerooms for code. If an attacker gets into the workshop, every product leaving it can be harmed. So you protect the whole workshop, not only the final product. Limit who may change things. Check where tools and parts come from. Keep passwords out of the code. Test the code both while it sits still and while it runs.

studyNotes.heading: Programming languages and libraries
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the raw materials of the software workshop, the languages and the ready-made parts.

A programming language shapes the risk. Source code is the set of human-written instructions. Compiled languages, such as C, are turned into machine code before they run, so customers usually receive only the machine code. Interpreted languages, such as Python, are read and run by another program, so the source code is often visible. Some languages sit in between. Java is compiled into an in-between form called bytecode, which a virtual machine then runs. Compiled programs are not secret either. A decompiler can turn them back into something readable, so never rely on hidden code to protect a password.

C and C plus plus let programmers control memory directly. That gives speed, but it also allows buffer overflows, where a program writes more data than a memory space can hold. Memory-safe languages, such as Java, C sharp and Rust, check or manage memory for the programmer. No language removes all flaws. Bad logic and injection can happen in any of them.

Think of two kitchens. In one, the knives are sharp and have no guards. An expert works very fast, and one slip is serious. In the other, the knives have guards. It is harder to cut yourself, but you can still burn the dinner.

A library is ready-made code that a program reuses. Think of buying pastry and not making your own. Most modern programs are mostly libraries. A flaw in a library becomes your flaw, and libraries pull in other libraries, so you may be using code that you have never heard of.

Here is a workplace example. A delivery company uses a free image library. A flaw is announced. Because the company pins its versions, meaning it names the exact version that it uses, it knows exactly what to update. So use approved sources, pin the version, verify what you download and keep libraries up to date.

Here is what to take away. Choose languages knowing their risks, and treat every library as part of your own product.

studyNotes.heading: Tool sets, the IDE and the runtime
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at the tools that build the software, and at the place where the software finally runs.

Tool sets include compilers, which turn source code into machine code, along with build tools and package managers, which fetch libraries. A poisoned tool can infect everything built with it. Think of a contaminated flour mill. Every bakery that buys the flour has a problem, however clean the bakery is.

So approve the tools you use, keep them patched and check their digital signatures or hashes. A hash is a short fingerprint of a file that changes if the file changes. A digital signature proves who issued the file and that it was not altered. There is also a risk called dependency confusion, where a package manager is tricked into fetching a public package with the same name as a private one. Using a private, controlled source helps to prevent it.

An integrated development environment, or IDE, is the program where developers write and debug code. Debugging means finding and fixing faults. Plug-ins add features to it. A bad plug-in can steal code or passwords, because it sits right beside both. In a workplace, allow only approved plug-ins, and manage them centrally. Also protect the developer's own computer, because it holds access to everything that matters.

The runtime is the environment where code executes. Examples are the Java Virtual Machine and containers. A container is a sealed package that holds an application and what it needs. Three controls matter most at runtime.

First, run software with least privilege, meaning only the access that it needs. A web application should not run as the all-powerful administrator. Second, patch the runtime and the container base images, the starting layers that a container is built from. Third, turn off debugging features in production, because they can reveal secrets and internal details.

Here is a workplace example. An online shop's container runs as the administrator with debugging switched on. An attacker who finds one small flaw now owns the whole system. Removing both problems greatly limits the harm.

Here is your takeaway. Trust no tool by default. Approve it, verify it, patch it, and run everything with least privilege.

studyNotes.heading: Continuous integration and continuous delivery
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the automatic production line that carries code from a developer's computer towards customers.

Continuous integration, often shortened to CI, means that developers merge code often, and each merge is built and tested automatically. Continuous delivery, often shortened to CD, keeps code ready to release, and a person approves the release. Continuous deployment goes one step further and releases automatically, with no person pressing the button.

The set of automatic steps is called a pipeline. Think of a bottling plant. Bottles move along a belt, and they are filled, checked and labeled by machines. A worker may press the final button to ship the batch. If someone tampers with the machine, every bottle is affected.

The pipeline holds the keys to production, so attackers want it. Controlling it is one of the most valuable things that a development organization can do. Here are the controls to remember.

- Limit who can edit the pipeline.
- Keep secrets in a protected vault.
- Sign what is built.
- Stop the build when security tests fail.
- Log every run.

Let me say why each one matters. A secret is a password, key or token. If it sits in a build script, anyone who can read the script has it. A vault is a protected store that hands out secrets only when they are needed. Signing what is built means that production can refuse anything which did not come from the real pipeline. Stopping the build makes security tests matter, because a warning that nobody has to act on is soon ignored.

Now here is a workplace walk-through. At a bank, a developer merges a change. The pipeline builds it and runs automatic tests. A security tool fails the build because of a known flaw in a library. The developer updates the library. The build passes and is signed. A manager approves the release. Because a person approves, this is continuous delivery and not continuous deployment. The pipeline logs every step, and those records go to a separate system.

Here is what to take away. The pipeline is a high-value target. Control who can change it, protect its secrets and let failed security tests stop the line.

studyNotes.heading: Configuration management and code repositories
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how a team keeps track of exactly what it has built, and where its code is stored.

Software configuration management, or SCM, records exactly which versions of code and settings make up each release. It lets you rebuild an old release or roll back to one. Its four classic parts, in order, are these.

- Configuration identification: naming and labeling each item.
- Configuration control: making sure that items change only in an authorized way.
- Configuration status accounting: recording the state and history of each item.
- Configuration audit: checking that what exists matches what the records say.

Think of a recipe book in a restaurant chain. Each dish has a version number. If customers fall ill, the chain can see exactly which recipe and which supplier were used that week.

Here is a workplace example. A release goes badly wrong on a Friday night. With good configuration management, the team knows exactly which versions made up last week's good release, and it can return to that within minutes. Without it, people guess.

A code repository stores code and its full history of changes. It is a very attractive target, because whoever can change the code can change the product. Protect it with least privilege, and with multifactor authentication, which means proof of identity by two or more kinds of evidence. Require peer review, so that a second person approves each change before it is merged. Sign commits where you can, a commit being one saved change. And keep backups.

Now for one of the most tested points. Never store passwords in code. Deleting a password from the latest version does not remove it from the history. Think of a page in a diary. Tearing out the newest page does not remove what you wrote in last year's volume. A leaked password must be changed first of all. Then you may clean the history, and add automatic secret scanning so that it does not happen again.

Here is your takeaway. Configuration management tells you exactly what you shipped. Repositories need strong access control and review, and any password committed to one must be treated as exposed.

studyNotes.heading: Static testing versus dynamic testing
studyNotes.body:
Next we come to the part the exam loves, how static and dynamic testing differ.

Static application security testing, or SAST, reads source code without running it. Static means standing still. Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, attacks the running application from outside. Dynamic means moving.

Think of inspecting a car. Static testing is walking around it in the garage with the engine off and reading the design. You can find a cracked part and say exactly where it is. Dynamic testing is driving it on the road. You discover that it pulls to the left at high speed, but you cannot say which bolt is responsible.

Let us take the strengths and the limits of each.

Static testing works early, even before the application can run. It can point to the exact line of code. It is a kind of white box testing, because the tester can see inside. Its limits are these. It produces many false alarms, which are warnings about problems that are not real. It needs tooling that understands the language. And it cannot see problems that appear only at run time, such as a wrongly configured server.

Dynamic testing needs a running application, so it comes later. It finds run-time and setup problems, and it does not need the source code, so it works on purchased software. It is a kind of black box testing, because the tester sees only the outside. Its limits are these. It cannot name the line of code, and it tests only what it manages to reach.

Here is a workplace example. A company has built a staff portal. Static testing in the first week finds a database query built unsafely, and it names the file and the line. Dynamic testing in the staging environment, a copy of production used for final checks, finds that the session cookie is sent without protection. Neither tool would have found the other's problem.

So use both. Each sees what the other misses. On the exam, if parts cannot run yet, choose static. If the source code is unavailable, choose dynamic.

Here is what to take away. Static reads code at rest and names the line. Dynamic attacks the running application and finds what only appears at run time.

studyNotes.heading: Interactive testing, composition analysis and fuzzing
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at the remaining kinds of testing, and at how to choose among them.

Interactive application security testing, or IAST, watches from inside the application while it is being tested. A small piece of monitoring software, called an agent, is placed inside the running application. While normal tests use the application, the agent watches what the code really does.

Think of a car with a mechanic's sensors attached to the engine while it is being driven. You get the road conditions of dynamic testing and the inside view of static testing. So interactive testing can report the exact line of code, with fewer false alarms. Its limits are these. It needs an agent that supports your language, and it can see only the code which the tests actually exercise. It runs in test environments. Do not confuse it with runtime application self-protection, which sits inside a production application and blocks attacks. Interactive testing finds. Self-protection defends.

Software composition analysis, or SCA, lists third-party components and their known flaws. It can also report their license terms. Think of a tool that reads the ingredients on a packet and checks them against a recall list. Composition analysis does not judge your own code. It is about what you borrowed. It can also produce a software bill of materials, a formal list of the components in a product.

Fuzzing feeds in random or unexpected input to cause failures. Mutation fuzzing changes valid input at random. Generation fuzzing builds input based on knowledge of the expected format. Fuzzing is especially good at finding crashes and memory errors.

Here is a simple way to choose, with a workplace example. A payment company uses each tool at its proper point.

- When code is saved, static testing and composition analysis run.
- In the test environment, interactive testing runs during the normal tests.
- In staging, dynamic testing attacks the complete application.
- For the file upload parser, fuzzing runs overnight.

As an adviser, remember that one tool never covers everything.

Here is your takeaway. Interactive testing watches from inside during tests, composition analysis checks borrowed parts, and fuzzing throws unexpected input to make software fail.

keyTerms.meaning: Integrated Development Environment: the program where developers write and debug code.
Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery: automatic building, testing and preparing of software for release.
Software Configuration Management: tracking the exact versions that make up each release.
A controlled store for code and its full change history.
Static Application Security Testing: examining code without running it.
Dynamic Application Security Testing: testing the application while it runs.
Software Composition Analysis: finding third-party components and their known flaws.
Sending random or unexpected input to make software fail.
The environment in which code executes.

keyPoints: Protect the whole software workshop, not only the final product.
SAST reads code at rest, while DAST tests the running application.
The CI/CD pipeline is a high-value target and needs strict access control.
A password committed to a repository stays in its history and must be changed.
Memory-safe languages reduce memory flaws but do not remove all flaws.
topics.memoryHook: Static is a parked car you inspect. Dynamic is the same car on the road.

question.prompt: A software company wants to find coding flaws as early as possible. Parts of its new product cannot yet be run. Which testing approach BEST meets this need?
options: Static application security testing of the source code
Dynamic application security testing of the staging site
Penetration testing of the production environment
Fuzz testing of the finished login service
question.explanation: Static testing reads source code, so the application does not need to run. Dynamic testing is tempting because it finds real run-time problems, but it needs a running application. The other two choices also need finished, running software.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team is about to write new firmware for a network device and wants to choose a language that greatly reduces the risk of buffer overflows. Which choice BEST meets this goal?
options: C, because it gives programmers direct control of memory
Assembly, because each instruction can be reviewed by hand
C plus plus, because it supports classes and object-oriented design
Rust, because it enforces memory safety
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rust enforces memory safety, which greatly reduces this kind of flaw. C is tempting because direct control sounds powerful, but that same control is what makes buffer overflows possible.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A product depends on many open libraries. The security team is worried that a new version of a library could silently add malicious code to the next build. What is the BEST control?
options: Always download the newest version during every build
Pin approved versions and verify their hashes
Copy code from public forums instead of using libraries
Let each developer choose the versions that work best
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pinning approved versions and checking their hashes stops an unexpected version from entering the build. Always using the newest version is tempting because it picks up fixes, but it also pulls in whatever was published last, without review.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A developer's plug-in for the integrated development environment is found sending source code to an unknown server. Which control would BEST prevent this from happening again?
options: Allow only approved plug-ins, managed centrally
Ask developers to read the reviews of each plug-in
Stop developers from using any such tool on their computers
Scan the production servers for signs of the plug-in
practiceQuestions.explanation: Central approval controls what can be installed, so it fixes the cause. Reading reviews is tempting and cheap, but reviews are no proof of safety and the decision is left to each person.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A review finds that a production web application runs in a container with full administrator rights and with debugging switched on. What is the BEST change?
options: Move the container to a larger host that has more memory
Keep debugging on, but limit who may read its output
Run it with least privilege and turn off debugging
Put a notice on the site telling users about the testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Least privilege limits the harm of any flaw, and removing debugging removes a source of leaked information. Limiting who reads the debug output is tempting, but the feature would still be active and could still be abused.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At a software company, each code change is automatically built and tested and is kept ready for release. A manager must approve before anything reaches production. What is this practice called?
options: Continuous deployment
Continuous delivery
Software composition analysis
Waterfall release control
practiceQuestions.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps code ready, and a person approves each release. Continuous deployment is tempting because the words are similar, but it releases automatically, with no person approving.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A build script holds a cloud administrator key in plain text, and every developer can edit the script. What should the security manager recommend?
options: Rename the variable so that the key is harder to find
Tell developers not to read the build script from now on
Encode the key in Base64 before storing it in the script
Move the key to a vault and restrict pipeline edits
practiceQuestions.explanation: A vault protects the secret, and limiting who may edit the pipeline protects the process. Base64 encoding is tempting because the key no longer looks readable, but encoding is not encryption and anyone can reverse it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: After a failed release, a team cannot tell which versions of code and settings made up the last good release, so it cannot roll back. Which practice is MOST clearly missing?
options: Threat modeling
Dynamic application testing
Software configuration management
Rate limiting
practiceQuestions.explanation: Software configuration management records exactly which versions make up each release. Dynamic testing is tempting because it was a failed release, but testing finds problems and does not keep a record of what was shipped.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has bought a web application and has no access to its source code. It wants to find server setup weaknesses and session handling problems in a staging copy. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Dynamic application security testing
Static application security testing
Software composition analysis of the source
Peer code review of the login module
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dynamic testing attacks the running application and needs no source code. Static testing is tempting because it is thorough, but it must be able to read the code, and it cannot see run-time setup problems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team wants security findings during its existing automated functional tests. It wants an agent inside the application to report the exact line of code, with few false alarms. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Static application security testing
Interactive application security testing
Software composition analysis of its packages
Manual penetration testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Interactive testing uses an agent inside the running application during tests, and can name the line of code. Static testing is tempting because it also names the line, but it does not run the application and it produces more false alarms.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An auditor asks which third-party packages inside a product have known flaws, and what license terms apply to them. Which tool would answer this MOST directly?
options: Fuzz testing of the input fields
Static analysis of the in-house code
Dynamic scanning of the login page
Software composition analysis
practiceQuestions.explanation: Software composition analysis identifies third-party components, their known flaws and their licenses. Static analysis is tempting because it reads code, but here it is aimed at the company's own code and not at what it borrowed.

topics.name: Assessing software security effectiveness
topics.simpleExplanation: How do you know your software security really works? You look for evidence. First, keep records of every change: who made it, what changed, when it happened and who approved it. Then compare those records with what was allowed. Second, study the risks in your software and decide what to do about each one. Some risks are reduced, some are shared, some are avoided and some are accepted. Management decides. Then check again, because an untested control is only a hope.

studyNotes.heading: Why we assess software security
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at why we must check that software security really works, and what counts as good proof.

Security controls can fail without anyone noticing. A test may be switched off to meet a deadline. A developer may find a way around review. A scanning tool may stop running after an upgrade, and nobody sees it. Assessment asks one simple question. Is the control working as intended, and what proves it?

Think of a shop owner. Having a cash register is not enough. The owner also compares the money in the till with the sales records at the end of the day. Without that daily count, a shortfall could go on for months.

There are three common kinds of proof, and they are not equally strong. The first is a statement, where somebody tells you that the control works. The second is a document, such as a policy that says what should happen. The third is direct evidence of what really did happen, such as protected logs and test results. Direct evidence is the strongest.

Here is a workplace example. A company's development manager says that every change is peer reviewed. The policy says so too. An assessor takes a sample of twenty recent changes and looks at the system records. Three have no second reviewer. The statement and the policy were both comforting, and neither was true for those three changes.

The independence of the assessor matters as well. People should not be the only ones to mark their own work. Internal audit, a separate team or an outside firm gives a more trustworthy view.

This objective of the exam outline names two things that you must be able to do. The first is auditing and logging of changes. The second is risk analysis and mitigation. Mitigation means reducing the risk. The rest of this topic takes these two in turn.

Here is what to take away. A control that has not been tested is only a hope. Ask for direct evidence, and have someone independent look at it.

studyNotes.heading: Auditing and logging of changes
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at what must be recorded every time software changes.

An audit trail is a record that lets someone trace what happened. Think of the visitors' book at a front desk, along with the guard's notes on who let each person in. For each software change, the record should show these things.

- Who made the change.
- What changed, including the old and new versions.
- When and where it happened.
- Who approved it, and which ticket or request it belongs to.
- Whether testing passed.

Let us take a workplace example. A change to an interest rate calculation goes live at a credit union. The record shows that a named developer changed one file. It shows the old and new versions of the code. It shows the time, the system involved, and the change request number. It shows that a different person approved it, and that the tests passed. If a customer complains six months later, the credit union can reconstruct the whole story.

Individual accounts matter here. Shared accounts break accountability, because you cannot prove who acted. If five developers all use one account for deployment, then the log only tells you that one of the five did it. Non-repudiation means that a person cannot believably deny an action. Individual accounts and strong authentication help to provide it. Digital signatures provide it more strongly.

Do not log everything without thought. Logs should not contain passwords, full card numbers or other secrets. A log that holds secrets becomes a target of its own.

Where do these records come from? They come from several places at once. The code repository records who changed what. The pipeline, the automatic line that builds and releases software, records each build and each release. The ticketing system records who asked and who approved. Production servers record what really arrived. An assessor joins these together to see the whole picture.

Here is your takeaway. For every change, record who, what, when, who approved and whether it passed its tests, and tie each action to one named person.

studyNotes.heading: Protecting the records and reviewing them
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how to keep those records trustworthy, and at how they should be reviewed.

If the people being logged can alter the logs, the logs prove very little. Think of a student marking the attendance register for himself. So send the records straight to a separate system that developers and administrators cannot alter. This often means a security information and event management system, or SIEM, which collects logs in one place and looks for patterns. Control who can read the records. Keep them as long as policy and law require. Use accurate, synchronized clocks, so that events on different systems can be placed in the right order.

Logs have no value if nobody reads them. Here are the review steps, using a monthly review at a retail company as a worked example.

Step one. Take the list of everything that reached production this month. Suppose there were 120 changes.

Step two. Take the list of approved change requests. Suppose there were 118.

Step three. Compare the two lists. Two changes have no matching request. Each one needs investigation. Who made it, what changed and why?

Step four. Sample the approved changes. Was the approver a different person from the author? Did the required tests and reviews really happen?

Step five. Check that emergency changes were reviewed afterward.

Step six. Report the results, and fix the cause of anything found. If a developer had direct access to production, remove that access.

Do not delete anything, and do not approve anything after the fact just to tidy up the records. An unexplained change could be an innocent mistake, or it could be an attack.

Also assess the results of security work over time. Useful measures include how long flaws stay open, how many flaws return after being fixed, and how many escape into production. A regression test is a repeat test that proves a fix did not break something else or bring an old flaw back.

Here is what to take away. Store logs where the people being logged cannot change them, and regularly compare what reached production with what was approved.

studyNotes.heading: Risk analysis in software
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how to decide which software flaws matter most.

Not every flaw can be fixed today. Risk analysis helps you to spend limited time on what counts. Think of a car with several faults. A worn seat cover can wait. Failing brakes cannot.

Threat modeling lists what could go wrong. One well-known way to organize the list is STRIDE. Its six letters stand for these.

- Spoofing: pretending to be someone else.
- Tampering: changing data without permission.
- Repudiation: denying that you did something.
- Information disclosure: exposing data.
- Denial of service: stopping real users from getting service.
- Elevation of privilege: gaining more access than allowed.

For flaws already known, there are public systems. Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVE, gives each publicly known flaw an identifying number. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, rates a flaw's severity from 0 to 10. In the current ratings, 0.1 to 3.9 is low, 4.0 to 6.9 is medium, 7.0 to 8.9 is high, and 9.0 to 10.0 is critical.

Severity is not the whole risk. Severity describes the flaw. Risk also depends on your own data, on your exposure, and on whether anyone is actually using the flaw in real attacks.

Here is a workplace example. A scan reports two flaws. Flaw A scores 9.8, but it sits on an isolated test machine with no real data. Flaw B scores 7.5, and it sits on an internet-facing payment system. With limited staff, the sensible choice is to deal with flaw B first, even though its score is lower.

That is the reasoning the exam wants. A scanner gives you a technical number. A manager and adviser turns it into a business decision.

Risk analysis can also be qualitative, which means using words such as high, medium and low, or quantitative, which means using money and numbers. The next part works through the numbers.

Here is your takeaway. Threat modeling finds what could go wrong, severity scores rate the flaw, and your own data and exposure decide the real risk.

studyNotes.heading: The numbers method, with a worked example
studyNotes.body:
Now we will work through the arithmetic of risk, one step at a time.

There are two formulas to know. Say them aloud.

Single loss expectancy equals asset value times exposure factor.

Annualized loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence.

Single loss expectancy, or SLE, is the cost of one event. The exposure factor is the share of the value lost in one event. The annualized rate of occurrence, or ARO, is how many times per year the event is expected. Annualized loss expectancy, or ALE, is the expected loss per year.

Think of a phone worth 400 dollars. One drop damages a quarter of its value, so one drop costs 100 dollars. If you drop it twice a year, you lose 200 dollars a year.

Now a workplace example. A shop's online system is worth 200,000 dollars. A flaw, if exploited, would damage 25 percent of its value.

Step one. 200,000 dollars times 0.25 is 50,000 dollars. That is the single loss expectancy.

Step two. The event is expected once every two years. That is 1 divided by 2, so the rate is 0.5 per year.

Step three. 50,000 dollars times 0.5 is 25,000 dollars. That is the annualized loss expectancy.

Now we can test whether a fix is worth buying. A fix costs 10,000 dollars a year, and it lowers the rate to 0.1 per year.

Step four. 50,000 dollars times 0.1 is 5,000 dollars. That is the new yearly loss.

Step five. Use this formula. The value of the fix equals the old yearly loss, minus the new yearly loss, minus the yearly cost of the fix. So 25,000 minus 5,000 is 20,000. Then 20,000 minus 10,000 is 10,000 dollars a year.

A positive answer means that the fix is worth buying. If the answer is negative, the fix costs more than it saves, on the numbers alone. The common mistake is to forget to subtract the cost of the fix.

Here is what to take away. Value times exposure gives one event. One event times the rate gives the yearly loss. Then subtract the new loss and the cost of the fix.

studyNotes.heading: Mitigation and decisions
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at what is done about a risk once it is understood, and who makes that decision.

There are four accepted responses to a risk. Learn all four.

- Mitigate: reduce the risk, for example by fixing the code.
- Transfer or share: move some of the financial impact, for example through insurance.
- Avoid: stop the risky activity or remove the feature.
- Accept: live with the risk, knowingly and in writing.

Think about a dangerous stretch of road on your way to work. You can drive slowly and wear a seat belt. That is mitigation. You can buy insurance. That is transfer. You can take a different road. That is avoidance. Or you can use the road anyway, fully aware of the danger. That is acceptance.

Ignoring a risk is never acceptable. Acceptance is a conscious and recorded decision. Ignoring it is simply pretending.

Here is a workplace example. An application has a rarely used file upload feature with a serious flaw. Rewriting it would be costly. The product owner checks, and very few people use it. Removing the feature is the cheapest and safest answer, and that is avoidance. A second flaw, in the main payment page, is fixed. That is mitigation. A third, minor flaw is low risk and cannot be fixed before launch. The business owner accepts it in writing, with a date for review.

The risk that is left after controls is called residual risk. Senior management owns the decision to accept it. Security staff and developers advise, and they should explain the risk in business terms. Developers should not quietly accept risk by deciding not to fix a flaw.

After a fix, test again to confirm that it worked. Then run regression tests to make sure that nothing else has broken. Keep a register of the risks, along with the owner of each and its review date, and go back to it, because threats and business needs both change.

Here is your takeaway. Choose among mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept. Senior management accepts residual risk, and every fix must be tested again.

keyTerms.meaning: A record that lets someone trace who did what and when.
Proof that stops a person from believably denying an action.
A repeat test showing that a change did not break anything or restore an old flaw.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a 0 to 10 rating of how severe a flaw is.
Single Loss Expectancy: the cost of one event, equal to asset value x exposure factor.
Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year an event is expected.
Annualized Loss Expectancy: expected yearly loss, equal to SLE x ARO.
The risk that remains after controls are applied.

keyPoints: Change logs must show who, what, when and who approved.
Store logs where the people being logged cannot alter them.
Compare production changes with approved requests.
Value of a fix is old ALE minus new ALE minus yearly fix cost.
Senior management decides whether to accept residual risk.
topics.memoryHook: Trust, but check the till. Controls need proof, just as a shop needs its daily count.

question.prompt: An auditor must decide whether changes to a live payroll application were properly authorized. Which evidence would BEST support this decision?
options: A signed statement from the development manager that the policy was followed
The results of a recent vulnerability scan of the payroll application
Protected deployment logs compared with the approved change requests
A copy of the written change management policy and its training records
question.explanation: Comparing protected logs with approved requests directly proves what happened. The signed statement is tempting, but it is only a claim and comes from someone with an interest in the result. A policy shows what should happen, not what did happen.

practiceQuestions.prompt: All of the developers at a company deploy software to production using one shared account. What is the MOST significant security problem with this?
options: It uses too much storage in the logging system
Actions cannot be traced to one person
It makes the deployment tool run more slowly
It breaks the clock synchronization of the servers
practiceQuestions.explanation: A shared account breaks accountability, because no one can prove who acted. The storage answer is tempting because the scenario is about logging, but the amount of log data is not the issue.

practiceQuestions.prompt: System administrators at a bank can edit the audit logs stored on the servers that they manage. What is the BEST way to make these records trustworthy?
options: Ask administrators to sign a code of conduct every year
Review the logs more often on those same servers
Send logs at once to a separate, protected system
Reduce the amount of detail recorded in each log
